Definition: The country's total international internet bandwidth capacity per internet user, indicating the quality and capacity of the country's connection to the global internet. Determined by submarine cable landings (for coastal states), cross-border terrestrial fibre (for landlocked states), and satellite links.
revision_notes: The cited ITU-sourced figure of 8.35 kbit/s per internet user (2016) falls within the 5-19 kbit/s band (code 2 = Low), not the <5 kbit/s band (code 1 = Very Low) originally assigned; the code has been corrected to match the cited figure on the metadata scale. No more recent ITU or World Bank international-bandwidth-per-user figures for Senegal were located despite targeted searches; 2016 remains the latest publicly available data point for this indicator.
revised_comments: Senegal's international internet bandwidth stood at 8.35 kbit/s per internet user in 2016, according to ITU data reported via TheGlobalEconomy.com, placing the country in the Low band (5-19 kbit/s per user). This remains the most recent internationally comparable figure publicly available for this indicator, as the ITU appears not to have published an updated per-user bandwidth estimate for Senegal since 2016.

Definition: Whether the country has enacted legal or regulatory requirements mandating that certain categories of data (personal data, government data, financial data, or critical infrastructure data) be stored within national borders. Central to data sovereignty debates in Africa.
revision_notes: Senegal's Loi n°2008-12 on personal data protection restricts cross-border transfers of personal data to jurisdictions lacking adequate protection (Arts. 49-50) but does not mandate that data be stored within national borders, supporting the original 'no localisation requirement' score. However, a BCEAO instruction covering credit bureaus (No. 009-06-2015) requires backup data to be held in another UMOA member state (a regional, not national, residency rule), and a 2024 BCEAO payment-services instruction imposes prior-notification and oversight requirements on outsourcing of critical operational functions by banks, payment institutions and e-money issuers; the sections read do not contain an explicit data-storage-location mandate. Secondary/promotional sources claim BCEAO now requires banking data to be hosted 'on national territory or in a UEMOA member state' and that the telecoms regulator (ARTP) requires call-detail-record data to be stored locally, but these claims could not be corroborated against primary regulatory text that was read directly. The score is retained on the strength of the primary data-protection law, but flagged for human review given indications of emerging sectoral (financial/telecoms) data-residency rules that a fuller reading of the BCEAO instrument corpus and ARTP regulations may substantiate.
revised_comments: Senegal has no general legal requirement mandating that personal, government or financial data be stored within national borders. Loi n°2008-12 on the protection of personal data instead restricts cross-border transfers of personal data to countries that do not guarantee an adequate level of protection, requiring prior notification to the Commission des Données Personnelles for such transfers, rather than prohibiting data leaving the country outright. Regional (UEMOA) financial-sector regulation from the BCEAO imposes information-security and outsourcing-notification obligations on banks, credit bureaus, payment institutions and e-money issuers operating in Senegal, with credit-bureau backup data required to be held in another UEMOA member state, but this falls short of a national data localisation mandate.
